title: Der Geist im Glas
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 99. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: KHM 99, a tale about the risks and rewards of curiosity. A poor woodcutter’s son, sent home from his studies when the money runs out, wanders off from the family’s timber-cutting and frees a spirit trapped in a glass bottle under an old oak’s roots — only to learn that the spirit, Mercurius, means to break his neck by way of thanks. The student tricks him back inside by demanding proof he ever fit in the bottle at all, then lets him out a second time for a fairer bargain: a rag that heals wounds and turns iron to silver, which clears the family’s debts and eventually makes the son the most famous doctor in the world.

sentences.t: Es war einmal ein armer Holzhacker, der arbeitete vom Morgen bis in die späte Nacht.
sentences.l: There was once a poor woodcutter, who worked from morning until late in the night.
sentences.i: There was once a poor woodcutter who worked from morning till late at night.
sentences.n: “Es war einmal” — literally “it was once” — is the fixed opening of a German tale, our “once upon a time.” Ein Holzhacker is a wood-chopper, the man who fells and splits wood for his living.

sentences.t: Als er sich endlich etwas Geld zusammengespart hatte, sprach er zu seinem Jungen „du bist mein einziges Kind, ich will das Geld, das ich mit saurem Schweiß erworben habe, zu deinem Unterricht anwenden;
sentences.l: When he had at last saved himself some money together, he spoke to his boy, “you are my only child, I will apply the money that I have earned with sour sweat to your schooling;
sentences.i: When at last he had saved a little money together, he said to his boy: “You are my only child; the money I earned with bitter sweat I mean to put toward your schooling;
sentences.n: zusammengespart shows how a separable verb builds its participle: the ge- slips in between particle and stem, zusammen-ge-spart. “mit saurem Schweiß” — with sour sweat — is the old phrase for hard-won earnings. Unterricht is instruction, teaching; the money is to pay for it.

sentences.t: lernst du etwas rechtschaffenes, so kannst du mich im Alter ernähren, wenn meine Glieder steif geworden sind, und ich daheim sitzen muß.“
sentences.l: if you learn something respectable, then you can feed me in old age, when my limbs have grown stiff, and I must sit at home.”
sentences.i: if you learn something honest, you will be able to keep me in my old age, when my limbs have grown stiff and I must sit at home.”
sentences.n: A conditional without wenn: German may simply put the verb first — “lernst du etwas” = “wenn du etwas lernst,” if you learn something — and the so that follows answers it. rechtschaffenes (modern rechtschaffen) is upright, honest; of a trade, respectable. ernähren is to nourish, to keep fed. “im Alter” is das Alter, old age — the noun, and not the adjective alt that the same letters begin.

sentences.t: Da gieng der Junge auf eine hohe Schule und lernte fleißig, so daß ihn seine Lehrer rühmten, und blieb eine Zeit lang dort.
sentences.l: Then the boy went to a high school and learned diligently, so that his teachers praised him, and remained there a length of time.
sentences.i: So the boy went off to a university and applied himself, so that his teachers praised him, and he stayed there a while.
sentences.n: “eine hohe Schule” is not a high school in our sense but the higher school, the university. gieng is the 1857 spelling of ging (went); the same ie runs through a whole family of these verbs — fieng, hieng. rühmen is to praise, to speak someone’s fame.

sentences.t: Als er ein paar Schulen durchgelernt hatte, doch aber noch nicht in allem vollkommen war, so war das bischen Armuth, das der Vater erworben hatte, drauf gegangen, und er mußte wieder zu ihm heim kehren.
sentences.l: When he had learned his way through a couple of schools, yet was still not perfect in everything, the little bit of poverty that the father had earned had gone on it, and he had to turn home again to him.
sentences.i: When he had worked his way through a couple of schools, and yet was not accomplished in everything, the small store the father had scraped together was spent, and he had to go home to him again.
sentences.n: Armuth (modern Armut, poverty) stands here for the pitiful little sum the father owned — his poverty is his property. “drauf gegangen” = darauf gegangen, gone on it, i.e. used up. durchlernen is separable: to get through a thing by learning.

sentences.t: „Ach,“ sprach der Vater betrübt, „ich kann dir nichts mehr geben und kann in der theuern Zeit auch keinen Heller mehr verdienen als das tägliche Brot.“
sentences.l: “Oh,” spoke the father sorrowfully, “I can give you nothing more, and in the dear time can earn no heller more than the daily bread.”
sentences.i: “Ah,” said the father sadly, “I can give you nothing more, and in this costly time I can earn not a farthing beyond the daily bread.”
sentences.n: Der Heller is the smallest copper coin, so “keinen Heller” is “not a penny.” theuern is the 1857 spelling of teuren; a dear time is a time of high prices. sprach is the old narrative past of sprechen, the ordinary verb of speech in these tales.

sentences.t: „Lieber Vater,“ antwortete der Sohn, „macht euch darüber keine Gedanken, wenns Gottes Wille also ist, so wirds zu meinem Besten ausschlagen; ich will mich schon drein schicken.“
sentences.l: “Dear father,” answered the son, “make yourselves no thoughts about it; if it is God’s will so, then it will turn out to my best; I will fit myself into it well enough.”
sentences.i: “Dear father,” answered the son, “do not trouble yourself over it; if such is God’s will, it will turn out for my best. I shall accommodate myself to it.”
sentences.n: The son addresses his father as ihr — macht euch — the older respectful plural used to a parent; English has only “you” for both. “sich drein schicken” (drein = darein) is the set phrase for resigning oneself, fitting in with what comes. wenns and wirds are the spoken clippings of wenn es and wird es.

sentences.t: Als der Vater hinaus in den Wald wollte, um etwas am Malterholz (am Zuhauen und Aufrichten) zu verdienen, so sprach der Sohn „ich will mit euch gehen und euch helfen.“
sentences.l: When the father wanted out into the wood, in order to earn something at the cord-wood (at the hewing and the setting-up), the son spoke, “I will go with you and help you.”
sentences.i: When the father was for going out into the forest, to earn something at the cord-wood — the cutting and the stacking — the son said: “I will go with you and help you.”
sentences.n: The round-bracket gloss “(am Zuhauen und Aufrichten)” is the Grimms’ own, printed in the 1857 text to explain a trade word to readers outside the region. Malterholz is firewood measured by the Malter, an old measure of volume; the work is hewing it to length and setting it up in stacks. German lets a modal stand without its verb of motion — “wollte hinaus,” wanted [to go] out.

sentences.t: „Ja, mein Sohn,“ sagte der Vater, „das sollte dir beschwerlich an kommen, du bist an harte Arbeit nicht gewöhnt, du hältst das nicht aus; ich habe auch nur eine Axt und kein Geld übrig, um noch eine zu kaufen.“
sentences.l: “Yes, my son,” said the father, “that would come hard upon you, you are not accustomed to hard work, you will not hold that out; I have besides only one axe and no money over to buy another.”
sentences.i: “Yes, my son,” said the father, “you would find it a burden; you are not used to hard work, you will not hold out. Besides, I have only the one axe and no money to spare for buying another.”
sentences.n: “ankommen” with a dative is to come upon someone, to strike them as — “das sollte dir beschwerlich ankommen,” that would come hard to you; the 1857 text writes the particle apart, an kommen. “aushalten” is to hold out, to endure. übrig is left over, to spare.

sentences.t: „Geht nur zum Nachbar,“ antwortete der Sohn, „der leiht euch seine Axt so lange, bis ich mir selbst eine verdient habe.“
sentences.l: “Just go to the neighbour,” answered the son, “he will lend you his axe for so long, until I have earned one for myself.”
sentences.i: “Only go to the neighbour,” answered the son; “he will lend you his axe until I have earned one of my own.”
sentences.n: nur in a command softens it to “just, only.” der at the head of the clause is a demonstrative — that one, the neighbour — the ordinary German way of picking up the person just named. leihen faces both ways, lending and borrowing; here it is lending.

sentences.t: Da borgte der Vater beim Nachbar eine Axt, und am andern Morgen, bei Anbruch des Tags, giengen sie zusammen hinaus in den Wald.
sentences.l: Then the father borrowed an axe from the neighbour, and on the next morning, at the breaking of the day, they went out together into the wood.
sentences.i: So the father borrowed an axe from the neighbour, and the next morning, at daybreak, they went out together into the forest.
sentences.n: borgen, like leihen, works in both directions — here it is borrowing. “bei Anbruch des Tags” = at the breaking of the day, daybreak; Tags is the old genitive.

sentences.t: Der Sohn half dem Vater und war ganz munter und frisch dabei.
sentences.l: The son helped the father and was quite lively and fresh at it.
sentences.i: The son helped his father, and was quite merry and brisk about it.
sentences.n: helfen takes the dative — dem Vater, not den Vater. dabei = at it, along with it; German uses these da- words where English would repeat the thing itself.

sentences.t: Als nun die Sonne über ihnen stand, sprach der Vater „wir wollen rasten und Mittag halten, hernach gehts noch einmal so gut.“
sentences.l: When now the sun stood over them, the father spoke, “we will rest and hold midday, afterwards it goes once again as well.”
sentences.i: When the sun stood right overhead, the father said: “Let us rest and take our noon meal; afterwards the work goes twice as well.”
sentences.n: “Mittag halten” is to keep midday, that is, to take the midday meal and the rest with it. “noch einmal so gut” = once again as good, the old way of saying twice as well. hernach = afterwards.

sentences.t: Der Sohn nahm sein Brot in die Hand und sprach „ruht euch nur aus, Vater, ich bin nicht müde, ich will in dem Wald ein wenig auf und abgehen und Vogelnester suchen.“
sentences.l: The son took his bread into his hand and spoke, “just rest yourselves out, father, I am not tired, I will go up and down a little in the wood and look for birds’ nests.”
sentences.i: The son took his bread in his hand and said: “Only rest yourself, father; I am not tired. I will walk up and down a little in the wood and look for birds’ nests.”
sentences.n: “sich ausruhen” is reflexive and separable — rest yourself out; euch is once more the respectful plural to his father. “auf und abgehen” is to go up and down, to stroll about.

sentences.t: „O du Geck,“ sprach der Vater, „was willst du da herum laufen, hernach bist du müde und kannst den Arm nicht mehr aufheben; bleib hier und setze dich zu mir.“
sentences.l: “Oh, you fool,” spoke the father, “what do you want to run about there, afterwards you are tired and can lift the arm no more; stay here and set yourself down by me.”
sentences.i: “Oh, you fool,” said the father, “why run about out there? Afterwards you will be tired and unable to lift your arm. Stay here and sit down by me.”
sentences.n: Ein Geck is a fool, a coxcomb, said half in exasperation. “was willst du da herum laufen” uses was where English says why. The father says du to his son while the son says ihr back to him — a difference English cannot carry, having only the one you.

sentences.t: Der Sohn aber gieng in den Wald, aß sein Brot, war ganz fröhlich und sah in die grünen Zweige hinein, ob er etwa ein Nest entdeckte.
sentences.l: The son, however, went into the wood, ate his bread, was quite merry and looked in among the green boughs, whether he might perhaps discover a nest.
sentences.i: But the son went off into the wood, ate his bread, and was quite merry, and looked in among the green boughs to see whether he might discover a nest.
sentences.n: “hineinsehen” is separable — sah … hinein, looked in. ob after a verb of looking means whether; German leaves out the “to see” that English wants. etwa = perhaps, by chance.

sentences.t: So gieng er hin und her, bis er endlich zu einer großen gefährlichen Eiche kam, die gewiß schon viele hundert Jahre alt war und die keine fünf Menschen umspannt hätten.
sentences.l: So he went hither and thither, until he came at last to a great, dangerous oak, which was surely already many hundred years old and which no five men could have spanned.
sentences.i: So he went to and fro, until at last he came to a great and fearsome oak, certainly many hundreds of years old, which five men together could not have reached around.
sentences.n: gefährlich here is closer to fearsome, formidable, than to dangerous — the tree is uncanny in its size. umspannen is to reach round with outstretched arms; hätten umspannt is the subjunctive of an unreal case, they would not have managed it.

sentences.t: Er blieb stehen und sah sie an und dachte „es muß doch mancher Vogel sein Nest hinein gebaut haben.“
sentences.l: He remained standing and looked at it and thought, “surely many a bird must have built its nest in there.”
sentences.i: He stood still and looked at it and thought: “Surely many a bird must have built its nest in there.”
sentences.n: “stehen bleiben” is to remain standing, that is, to stop. “ansehen” is separable — sah … an, looked at. doch inside the thought carries the force of “surely.” mancher = many a.

sentences.t: Da däuchte ihn auf einmal als hörte er eine Stimme.
sentences.l: Then it seemed to him all at once as though he heard a voice.
sentences.n: däuchte, from dünken (to seem), is an old impersonal past with the person in the accusative — ihn däuchte, “it seemed him.” Modern German says es schien ihm. “auf einmal” = all at once, suddenly.

sentences.t: Er horchte und vernahm wie es mit so einem recht dumpfen Ton rief „laß mich heraus, laß mich heraus.“
sentences.l: He listened and perceived how it called with such a really hollow tone, “let me out, let me out.”
sentences.i: He listened, and made out how something called in a dull, muffled tone: “Let me out, let me out.”
sentences.n: vernehmen is to catch, to make out by ear. dumpf is dull, muffled, without ring. The cry “laß mich heraus” comes back again and again in this tale; heraus is out, toward the speaker.

sentences.t: Er sah sich rings um, konnte aber nichts entdecken, doch es war ihm als ob die Stimme unten aus der Erde hervor käme.
sentences.l: He looked round about himself, but could discover nothing, yet it was to him as though the voice came forth from below out of the earth.
sentences.i: He looked all about him, but could discover nothing; yet it seemed to him as if the voice came up out of the earth below.
sentences.n: “sich umsehen” is reflexive and separable — sah sich … um; rings adds “round about.” käme is the subjunctive that regularly follows als ob, marking how a thing seemed rather than how it was.

sentences.t: Da rief er „wo bist du?“
sentences.l: Then he called, “where are you?”
sentences.n: du is the plain familiar you, used throughout: he addresses the unseen voice without ceremony, and it answers him in the same way.

sentences.t: Die Stimme antwortete „ich stecke da unten bei den Eichwurzeln.
sentences.l: The voice answered, “I am stuck down there by the oak-roots.
sentences.i: The voice answered: “I am lodged down there among the oak roots.
sentences.n: stecken is to be stuck, wedged fast in something — the spirit is not merely lying there. Eichwurzeln is a plain compound, Eiche + Wurzeln, oak-roots.

sentences.t: Laß mich heraus, laß mich heraus.“
sentences.l: Let me out, let me out.”
sentences.n: The same cry as before, now from the thing itself. laß (modern lass) is the imperative of lassen, to let.

sentences.t: Der Schüler fieng an unter dem Baum aufzuräumen und bei den Wurzeln zu suchen, bis er endlich in einer kleinen Höhlung eine Glasflasche entdeckte.
sentences.l: The scholar began to clear away under the tree and to search by the roots, until at last he discovered a glass bottle in a small hollow.
sentences.i: The student set about clearing away under the tree and searching among the roots, until at last, in a little hollow, he discovered a glass bottle.
sentences.n: Schüler is anyone under instruction — here the student home from his schools, and the tale calls him this from now on. “anfangen” is separable, fieng an, and the zu of the following infinitive slips inside aufzuräumen, itself a separable verb. fieng is the 1857 spelling of fing.

sentences.t: Er hob sie in die Höhe und hielt sie gegen das Licht, da sah er ein Ding, gleich einem Frosch gestaltet, das sprang darin auf und nieder.
sentences.l: He lifted it into the height and held it against the light; then he saw a thing, shaped like a frog, that sprang up and down inside it.
sentences.i: He lifted it up and held it against the light, and then he saw a thing shaped like a frog, springing up and down inside.
sentences.n: “in die Höhe heben” is the ordinary way of saying to lift up. “gleich einem Frosch gestaltet” = formed like a frog, with gleich taking the dative. darin = in it, in there.

sentences.t: „Laß mich heraus, laß mich heraus,“ riefs von neuem, und der Schüler, der an nichts Böses dachte, nahm den Pfropfen von der Flasche ab.
sentences.l: “Let me out, let me out,” it called anew, and the scholar, who thought of nothing evil, took the stopper off the bottle.
sentences.i: “Let me out, let me out,” it cried again; and the student, thinking no harm, took the stopper off the bottle.
sentences.n: riefs = rief es, with the pronoun clipped onto the verb. “von neuem” = anew, again. “abnehmen” is separable — nahm … ab, took off — and the particle waits at the end of the clause, which is the ordinary German pattern.

sentences.t: Alsbald stieg ein Geist heraus und fieng an zu wachsen, und wuchs so schnell, daß er in wenigen Augenblicken als ein entsetzlicher Kerl, so groß wie der halbe Baum, vor dem Schüler stand.
sentences.l: Straightway a spirit climbed out and began to grow, and grew so fast that in a few moments he stood before the scholar as a frightful fellow, as big as the half tree.
sentences.i: At once a spirit rose out of it and began to grow, and grew so fast that within a few moments he stood before the student as a terrible fellow, half as tall as the tree.
sentences.n: Geist is spirit in the sense of a supernatural being, not the ghost of a dead man. alsbald = straightway, at once. Kerl is a fellow, said of a big rough man. daß is the 1857 spelling of dass.

sentences.t: „Weißt du,“ rief er mit einer fürchterlichen Stimme, „was dein Lohn dafür ist, daß du mich heraus gelassen hast?“
sentences.l: “Do you know,” he cried with a fearful voice, “what your reward is for it, that you have let me out?”
sentences.i: “Do you know,” he cried in a terrible voice, “what your reward is for having let me out?”
sentences.n: “dafür, daß …” is the regular German frame — for it, that … — where English says “for having ….” Lohn is wages, reward, and the spirit means it grimly.

sentences.t: „Nein,“ antwortete der Schüler ohne Furcht, „wie soll ich das wissen?“
sentences.l: “No,” answered the scholar without fear, “how should I know that?”
sentences.n: The boy is unafraid from the first, and that is what saves him. “ohne Furcht” = without fear.

sentences.t: „So will ich dirs sagen,“ rief der Geist, „den Hals muß ich dir dafür brechen.“
sentences.l: “Then I will tell it to you,” cried the spirit, “the neck I must break you for it.”
sentences.i: “Then I will tell you,” cried the spirit: “for that I must break your neck.”
sentences.n: German says the neck and puts the owner in the dative — “muß ich dir den Hals brechen,” I must break the neck to you. This dative of the person is the ordinary way of speaking about someone’s body. dirs = dir es.

sentences.t: „Das hättest du mir früher sagen sollen,“ antwortete der Schüler, „so hätte ich dich stecken lassen; mein Kopf aber soll vor dir wohl feststehen, da müssen mehr Leute gefragt werden.“
sentences.l: “That you should have told me earlier,” answered the scholar, “then I would have let you stay stuck; my head, however, shall stand fast before you well enough, there more people must be asked.”
sentences.i: “You should have told me that sooner,” answered the student; “then I would have left you where you were. But my head will stand firm enough against you — more than one has a say in that.”
sentences.n: “stecken lassen” is to leave a thing stuck where it is. feststehen is to stand fast; the boy means his head is not so easily taken. “da müssen mehr Leute gefragt werden” is a proverbial refusal: the matter is not yours alone to settle.

sentences.t: „Mehr Leute hin, mehr Leute her,“ rief der Geist, „deinen verdienten Lohn den sollst du haben.
sentences.l: “More people hither, more people thither,” cried the spirit, “your earned reward, that you shall have.
sentences.i: “More people this way, more people that,” cried the spirit; “your earned reward you shall have.
sentences.n: “X hin, X her” is a set brush-off — never mind your X. The sentence names the object first and then picks it up again with den, a common way of throwing weight on it: your reward — that is what you shall have.

sentences.t: Denkst du, ich wäre aus Gnade da so lange Zeit eingeschlossen worden, nein, es war zu meiner Strafe;
sentences.l: Do you think I was shut in there so long a time out of grace? no, it was for my punishment;
sentences.i: Do you think I was shut up in there all that time as a kindness? No, it was for my punishment;
sentences.n: Gnade is grace, favour — “aus Gnade” = as an act of mercy. “eingeschlossen worden” is a past passive: was shut in. German runs the question and its answer together with a comma where English wants a question mark.

sentences.t: ich bin der großmächtige Merkurius, wer mich losläßt, dem muß ich den Hals brechen.“
sentences.l: I am the great and mighty Merkurius; whoever lets me loose, to him I must break the neck.”
sentences.i: I am the great and mighty Merkurius; whoever sets me free, his neck I must break.”
sentences.n: Merkurius is the Latin name of the god Mercury, borrowed here for a bound spirit of great power; it stands as a name and is left untranslated. “wer …, dem …” pairs an indefinite relative with the pronoun that answers it — whoever …, to that one …. “loslassen” is separable, to let loose.

sentences.t: „Sachte,“ antwortete der Schüler, „so geschwind geht das nicht, erst muß ich auch wissen daß du wirklich in der kleinen Flasche gesessen hast und daß du der rechte Geist bist:
sentences.l: “Gently,” answered the scholar, “that does not go so quickly, first I must also know that you really sat in the little bottle and that you are the right spirit:
sentences.i: “Softly,” answered the student, “it does not go so fast as that; first I must know that you really did sit in the little bottle, and that you are the spirit you claim to be:
sentences.n: sachte is “gently, not so fast” — a word for reining someone in. geschwind = quickly. “der rechte Geist” is the right one, the genuine one.

sentences.t: kannst du auch wieder hinein, so will ichs glauben, und dann magst du mit mir anfangen was du willst.“
sentences.l: if you can get in again too, then I will believe it, and then you may begin with me what you will.”
sentences.i: if you can get back in again, then I will believe it, and then you may do with me what you please.”
sentences.n: Another conditional without wenn — “kannst du auch wieder hinein” = if you can [get] in again; the verb of motion is left out after the modal, and English has to supply it. “mit jemandem anfangen” is to start in on someone, to do with them as one likes.

sentences.t: Der Geist sprach voll Hochmuth „das ist eine geringe Kunst,“ zog sich zusammen und machte sich so dünn und klein, wie er anfangs gewesen war, also daß er durch dieselbe Öffnung und durch den Hals der Flasche wieder hinein kroch.
sentences.l: The spirit spoke full of haughtiness, “that is a slight art,” drew himself together and made himself as thin and small as he had been at first, so that he crept in again through the same opening and through the neck of the bottle.
sentences.i: The spirit said in his pride, “That is a small feat,” and drew himself together and made himself as thin and small as he had been at first, so that he crept back in through the same opening and through the neck of the bottle.
sentences.n: Hochmuth (modern Hochmut) is high-mindedness in the bad sense, arrogance — and it is what undoes him. “eine geringe Kunst” is a slight art, no great trick. Der Hals is both a person’s neck and a bottle’s, which is why the spirit’s threat and the bottle’s neck are the same word.

sentences.t: Kaum aber war er darin, so drückte der Schüler den abgezogenen Pfropfen wieder auf und warf die Flasche unter die Eichwurzeln an ihren alten Platz, und der Geist war betrogen.
sentences.l: Hardly, however, was he inside, when the scholar pressed the drawn-off stopper on again and threw the bottle under the oak-roots into its old place, and the spirit was deceived.
sentences.i: But scarcely was he inside when the student pressed the stopper back on and threw the bottle under the oak roots into its old place — and the spirit was tricked.
sentences.n: “Kaum …, so …” is the old pairing for “no sooner … than”; kaum at the front pulls the verb ahead of its subject. “aufdrücken” is separable, to press on. abgezogen is the participle of abziehen, to draw off, used here as an adjective for the stopper.

sentences.t: Nun wollte der Schüler zu seinem Vater zurückgehen, aber der Geist rief ganz kläglich „ach, laß mich doch heraus, laß mich doch heraus.“
sentences.l: Now the scholar wanted to go back to his father, but the spirit cried quite piteously, “oh, do let me out, do let me out.”
sentences.i: Now the student was for going back to his father, but the spirit cried most piteously: “Oh, do let me out, do let me out!”
sentences.n: kläglich is plaintive, pitiful — the same voice that was threatening him a moment before. doch in a request is the pleading particle English carries with “do.”

sentences.t: „Nein,“ antwortete der Schüler, „zum zweitenmale nicht: wer mir einmal nach dem Leben gestrebt hat, den laß ich nicht los, wenn ich ihn wieder eingefangen habe.“
sentences.l: “No,” answered the scholar, “not for the second time: whoever has once striven after my life, him I do not let loose, when I have caught him again.”
sentences.i: “No,” answered the student, “not a second time. Whoever has once sought my life, him I do not let go once I have caught him again.”
sentences.n: “jemandem nach dem Leben streben” is the set phrase for seeking someone’s life. zum zweitenmale (modern zum zweiten Male) = for the second time. “einfangen” is separable, to catch and shut up.

sentences.t: „Wenn du mich frei machst,“ rief der Geist, „so will ich dir so viel geben, daß du dein Lebtag genug hast.“
sentences.l: “If you make me free,” cried the spirit, “then I will give you so much that you have enough your life-day long.”
sentences.i: “If you set me free,” cried the spirit, “I will give you so much that you will have enough all your life long.”
sentences.n: “dein Lebtag” is an old adverbial accusative — for your life-day, that is, as long as you live; the phrase does not change its form.

sentences.t: „Nein,“ antwortete der Schüler, „du würdest mich betriegen wie das erstemal.“
sentences.l: “No,” answered the scholar, “you would deceive me like the first time.”
sentences.n: betriegen is the older spelling of betrügen, to deceive; the same ie/ü pair shows up in a few verbs of this age. “das erstemal” (modern das erste Mal) stands in the bare accusative as a phrase of time.

sentences.t: „Du verscherzest dein Glück,“ sprach der Geist, „ich will dir nichts thun, sondern dich reichlich belohnen.“
sentences.l: “You are trifling away your luck,” spoke the spirit, “I will do you nothing, but rather reward you richly.”
sentences.i: “You are throwing away your good fortune,” said the spirit; “I will do you no harm, but reward you richly.”
sentences.n: verscherzen is to lose a thing by frivolity, to forfeit it through one’s own doing. thun is the 1857 spelling of tun, to do; gethan for getan comes later in the tale. sondern is the “but” that corrects a preceding negative.

sentences.t: Der Schüler dachte „ich wills wagen, vielleicht hält er Wort, und anhaben soll er mir doch nichts.“
sentences.l: The scholar thought, “I will risk it, perhaps he keeps his word, and harm me he shall not, at any rate.”
sentences.i: The student thought: “I will risk it. Perhaps he will keep his word — and in any case he shall be able to do me no harm.”
sentences.n: “jemandem etwas anhaben” is to be able to do someone harm. The infinitive is thrown to the front here — “anhaben soll er mir doch nichts” — which is emphasis, not disorder. wills = will es.

sentences.t: Da nahm er den Pfropfen ab, und der Geist stieg wie das vorigemal heraus, dehnte sich auseinander, und ward groß wie ein Riese.
sentences.l: Then he took the stopper off, and the spirit climbed out as the previous time, stretched himself apart, and became big as a giant.
sentences.i: So he took off the stopper, and the spirit rose out as before, stretched himself out, and grew as big as a giant.
sentences.n: ward is the old past of werden, became, which the tales use constantly where modern German has wurde. “sich auseinander dehnen” is to stretch oneself apart, to expand.

sentences.t: „Nun sollst du deinen Lohn haben,“ sprach er, und reichte dem Schüler einen kleinen Lappen, ganz wie ein Pflaster, und sagte „wenn du mit dem einen Ende eine Wunde bestreichst, so heilt sie:
sentences.l: “Now you shall have your reward,” he spoke, and handed the scholar a small rag, quite like a plaster, and said, “if you stroke a wound with the one end, then it heals:
sentences.i: “Now you shall have your reward,” he said, and handed the student a little rag, just like a plaster, and told him: “If you stroke a wound with the one end, it heals;
sentences.n: Ein Pflaster is a dressing laid on a wound, a plaster; the gift is a strip of cloth that works like one. bestreichen is to stroke over, to smear along. Another wenn-clause answered by so, as throughout this tale.

sentences.t: und wenn du mit dem andern Ende Stahl und Eisen bestreichst, so wird es in Silber verwandelt.“
sentences.l: and if you stroke steel and iron with the other end, then it is turned into silver.”
sentences.n: “in Silber verwandelt werden” is a passive: is transformed into silver. It is this second power, and not the healing, that drives the rest of the tale. Stahl is the noun, steel — not a form of stehlen, to steal, which the same letters spell.

sentences.t: „Das muß ich erst versuchen,“ sprach der Schüler, gieng an einen Baum, ritzte die Rinde mit seiner Axt und bestrich sie mit dem einen Ende des Pflasters: alsbald schloß sie sich wieder zusammen und war geheilt.
sentences.l: “That I must first try,” spoke the scholar, went to a tree, scratched the bark with his axe and stroked it with the one end of the plaster: straightway it closed itself together again and was healed.
sentences.i: “I must try that first,” said the student, and went to a tree, scored the bark with his axe and stroked it with the one end of the plaster; at once it closed up again and was healed.
sentences.n: ritzen is to scratch, to score. “sich zusammenschließen” is reflexive and separable — closed itself together again. The bark is treated as a wound, which is the point of the test. schloß here is the past of schließen, to close, and not das Schloß, a castle.

sentences.t: „Nun, es hat seine Richtigkeit,“ sprach er zum Geist, „jetzt können wir uns trennen.“
sentences.l: “Well, it has its correctness,” he spoke to the spirit, “now we can part ourselves.”
sentences.i: “Well, the thing holds good,” he said to the spirit; “now we can part.”
sentences.n: “es hat seine Richtigkeit” is a set phrase: it is in order, it is as it should be. “sich trennen” is reflexive where English simply parts.

sentences.t: Der Geist dankte ihm für seine Erlösung, und der Schüler dankte dem Geist für sein Geschenk und gieng zurück zu seinem Vater.
sentences.l: The spirit thanked him for his release, and the scholar thanked the spirit for his gift and went back to his father.
sentences.n: danken takes the dative — dankte ihm, dankte dem Geist. Erlösung is release, redemption, the word these tales use for the freeing of an enchanted or bound being.

sentences.t: „Wo bist du herum gelaufen?“ sprach der Vater, „warum hast du die Arbeit vergessen?
sentences.l: “Where have you been running about?” spoke the father, “why have you forgotten the work?
sentences.i: “Where have you been running about?” said the father. “Why have you forgotten the work?
sentences.n: “herumlaufen” is separable, to run about; its participle keeps the particle in front, herumgelaufen, though the 1857 text writes it apart. The speech tag sits between the two questions, as it often does in these tales.

sentences.t: Ich habe es ja gleich gesagt daß du nichts zu Stande bringen würdest.“
sentences.l: I said it at once, indeed, that you would bring nothing to a stand.”
sentences.i: I said so from the first, that you would get nothing done.”
sentences.n: “zu Stande bringen” (modern zustande bringen) is to bring a thing about, to accomplish it. ja inside a sentence is not “yes” but an appeal to what both know already: I did say so.

sentences.t: „Gebt euch zufrieden, Vater, ich wills nachholen.“
sentences.l: “Give yourselves content, father, I will make it up.”
sentences.i: “Be content, father; I will make it up.”
sentences.n: “sich zufrieden geben” is to be satisfied, to let a thing rest. Gebt … euch is the respectful plural again. nachholen is to fetch up afterwards, to make good what was missed.

sentences.t: „Ja, nachholen,“ sprach der Vater zornig, „das hat keine Art.“
sentences.l: “Yes, make it up,” spoke the father angrily, “that has no manner.”
sentences.i: “Yes, make it up!” said the father angrily. “That is no way to go on.”
sentences.n: “das hat keine Art” is a set expression of disapproval: that is unseemly, that will not do. The father throws the son’s own word back at him in scorn.

sentences.t: „Habt acht, Vater, den Baum da will ich gleich umhauen, daß er krachen soll.“
sentences.l: “Take heed, father, that tree there I will hew down at once, so that it shall crack.”
sentences.i: “Take heed, father — that tree there I will cut down straight away, so that it shall come down with a crash.”
sentences.n: “acht haben” is to pay heed. The object stands first — “den Baum da will ich …” — which German allows freely, throwing the weight onto the tree. umhauen is separable, to hew down.

sentences.t: Da nahm er sein Pflaster, bestrich die Axt damit und that einen gewaltigen Hieb: aber weil das Eisen in Silber verwandelt war, so legte sich die Schneide um.
sentences.l: Then he took his plaster, stroked the axe with it and did a mighty blow: but because the iron had been turned into silver, the edge laid itself over.
sentences.i: So he took his plaster, stroked the axe with it and struck a mighty blow; but because the iron had been turned into silver, the edge bent over.
sentences.n: “einen Hieb thun” is to deal a blow, with thun (modern tun) where English says strike. “sich umlegen” is reflexive and separable — the blade lays itself over, that is, it folds. Silver is soft, and that is the whole point. die Schneide is the cutting edge of the blade, the noun from schneiden.

sentences.t: „Ei, Vater, seht einmal, was habt ihr mir für eine schlechte Axt gegeben, die ist ganz schief geworden.“
sentences.l: “Ei, father, look once, what a bad axe have you given me, it has become quite crooked.”
sentences.i: “Why, father, just look what a poor axe you gave me; it has gone quite crooked.”
sentences.n: “was für eine …” is the German frame for “what a …,” and it may be split, as here, with für standing apart from was. einmal after an imperative softens it to “just.” Ei is a mild cry of surprise.

sentences.t: Da erschrack der Vater und sprach „ach, was hast du gemacht! nun muß ich die Axt bezahlen und weiß nicht womit; das ist der Nutzen, den ich von deiner Arbeit habe.“
sentences.l: Then the father took fright and spoke, “oh, what have you done! now I must pay for the axe and do not know with what; that is the profit which I have from your work.”
sentences.i: Then the father took fright and said: “Oh, what have you done! Now I must pay for the axe and do not know with what. That is the good I get of your work.”
sentences.n: erschrack (modern erschrak) is the past of erschrecken, to take fright. womit = with what; German fastens the preposition onto the question-word. Nutzen is use, profit, said here bitterly.

sentences.t: „Werdet nicht bös,“ antwortete der Sohn, „die Axt will ich schon bezahlen.“
sentences.l: “Do not become angry,” answered the son, “the axe I will pay for well enough.”
sentences.i: “Do not be angry,” answered the son; “I will pay for the axe, never fear.”
sentences.n: bös (modern böse) is here angry rather than wicked. schon in a promise means “sure enough, never fear,” not “already.”

sentences.t: „O, du Dummbart,“ rief der Vater, „wovon willst du sie bezahlen? du hast nichts als was ich dir gebe; das sind Studentenkniffe, die dir im Kopf stecken, aber vom Holzhacken hast du keinen Verstand.“
sentences.l: “Oh, you blockhead,” cried the father, “from what will you pay for it? you have nothing but what I give you; those are student’s tricks that stick in your head, but of woodcutting you have no understanding.”
sentences.i: “Oh, you dolt,” cried the father, “what will you pay for it with? You have nothing but what I give you. Those are students’ tricks lodged in your head; but of woodcutting you understand nothing.”
sentences.n: Dummbart is a coined name of abuse — dumm plus Bart, roughly “dull-beard,” a blockhead. wovon = from what, out of what. Studentenkniffe are the dodges a student picks up; ein Kniff is a sleight, a trick. Verstand is the noun, understanding: “von etwas keinen Verstand haben” is to know nothing of a thing.

sentences.t: Über ein Weilchen sprach der Schüler „Vater, ich kann doch nichts mehr arbeiten, wir wollen lieber Feierabend machen.“
sentences.l: After a little while the scholar spoke, “father, I can work nothing more, we will rather make evening-rest.”
sentences.i: After a little while the student said: “Father, I can do no more work; let us rather leave off for the day.”
sentences.n: “über ein Weilchen” = after a little while; Weilchen is the diminutive of Weile. “Feierabend machen” is to stop work for the day — der Feierabend is the evening that belongs to rest and not to the trade.

sentences.t: „Ei was,“ antwortete er, „meinst du ich wollte die Hände in den Schooß legen wie du? ich muß noch schaffen, du kannst dich aber heim packen.“
sentences.l: “Ei what,” he answered, “do you think I would lay the hands in the lap like you? I must still work, you, however, can pack yourself off home.”
sentences.i: “What nonsense,” he answered, “do you think I would sit with my hands in my lap as you do? I must go on working; but you can take yourself off home.”
sentences.n: “die Hände in den Schoß legen” is the set image for idling. Schooß is the 1857 spelling of Schoß, the lap. “sich heim packen” is reflexive and rough — take yourself off. wollte is a subjunctive here: would.

sentences.t: „Vater, ich bin zum erstenmal hier in dem Wald, ich weiß den Weg nicht allein, geht doch mit mir.“
sentences.l: “Father, I am for the first time here in the wood, I do not know the way alone, do go with me.”
sentences.i: “Father, this is my first time here in the wood; I do not know the way by myself — do come with me.”
sentences.n: The son is lying, and it works: this is the one thing that will move his father. zum erstenmal (modern zum ersten Mal) = for the first time. doch in the request is again the pleading particle. der Weg is the noun, the way; the same letters small are weg, away.

sentences.t: Weil sich der Zorn gelegt hatte, so ließ der Vater sich endlich bereden und gieng mit ihm heim.
sentences.l: Because the anger had laid itself, the father let himself at last be persuaded and went home with him.
sentences.i: Since his anger had settled, the father at last let himself be talked round, and went home with him.
sentences.n: “sich legen,” of wind or anger or noise, is to subside — to lay itself. “sich bereden lassen” is to let oneself be talked into a thing; lassen with an infinitive is German’s regular way of forming this.

sentences.t: Da sprach er zum Sohn „geh und verkauf die verschändete Axt und sieh zu was du dafür kriegst; das übrige muß ich verdienen, um sie dem Nachbar zu bezahlen.“
sentences.l: Then he spoke to the son, “go and sell the ruined axe and see to what you get for it; the rest I must earn, in order to pay it to the neighbour.”
sentences.i: Then he said to his son: “Go and sell the spoiled axe and see what you get for it; the rest I must earn, to pay the neighbour for it.”
sentences.n: verschändet is a strong word — disfigured, ruined, from schänden, to disgrace. “zusehen” is separable, to see to a thing. kriegen is the everyday verb for getting.

sentences.t: Der Sohn nahm die Axt und trug sie in die Stadt zu einem Goldschmied, der probierte sie, legte sie auf die Wage und sprach „sie ist vierhundert Thaler werth, so viel habe ich nicht baar.“
sentences.l: The son took the axe and carried it into the town to a goldsmith, who tested it, laid it on the scales and spoke, “it is worth four hundred thaler, so much I do not have in cash.”
sentences.i: The son took the axe and carried it into the town to a goldsmith, who tested it, laid it on the scales and said: “It is worth four hundred thalers; so much I have not by me in ready money.”
sentences.n: Der Thaler (modern Taler) is the large silver coin of the old German states, and four hundred of them are a fortune to this household. baar (modern bar) is cash, coin in hand. Wage is the 1857 spelling of Waage, the balance.

sentences.t: Der Schüler sprach „gebt mir was ihr habt, das übrige will ich euch borgen.“
sentences.l: The scholar spoke, “give me what you have, the rest I will lend you.”
sentences.i: The student said: “Give me what you have; the rest I will let you owe me.”
sentences.n: borgen faces both ways in German, and here it is the boy who lends, leaving the goldsmith in his debt. He addresses the goldsmith as ihr, the older polite plural.

sentences.t: Der Goldschmied gab ihm dreihundert Thaler und blieb einhundert schuldig.
sentences.l: The goldsmith gave him three hundred thaler and remained one hundred owing.
sentences.i: The goldsmith gave him three hundred thalers and remained a hundred in his debt.
sentences.n: “schuldig bleiben” is to stay owing — the regular phrase for a debt left standing.

sentences.t: Darauf gieng der Schüler heim und sprach „Vater, ich habe Geld, geht und fragt was der Nachbar für die Axt haben will.“
sentences.l: Thereupon the scholar went home and spoke, “father, I have money, go and ask what the neighbour wants to have for the axe.”
sentences.i: Thereupon the student went home and said: “Father, I have money; go and ask what the neighbour wants for the axe.”
sentences.n: darauf = thereupon, upon that. geht and fragt are once more the respectful plural imperatives to his father.

sentences.t: „Das weiß ich schon,“ antwortete der Alte, „einen Thaler, sechs Groschen.“
sentences.l: “That I know already,” answered the old man, “one thaler, six groschen.”
sentences.n: der Alte, “the old one,” is simply the old man, the father. Der Groschen is a small silver coin; a thaler and six groschen is a modest price for a good axe.

sentences.t: „So gebt ihm zwei Thaler zwölf Groschen, das ist das Doppelte und ist genug; seht ihr, ich habe Geld im Überfluß,“
sentences.l: “Then give him two thaler twelve groschen, that is the double and is enough; you see, I have money in overflow,”
sentences.i: “Then give him two thalers and twelve groschen — that is double, and enough. You see, I have money in plenty,”
sentences.n: “im Überfluß” is in overflow, in abundance. seht ihr is the polite plural “you see.” Paying twice the price is the son’s way of settling the debt handsomely.

sentences.t: und gab dem Vater einhundert Thaler und sprach „es soll euch niemals fehlen, lebt nach eurer Bequemlichkeit.“
sentences.l: and gave the father one hundred thaler and spoke, “it shall never be lacking to you, live according to your comfort.”
sentences.i: and he gave his father a hundred thalers and said: “You shall never want for anything; live at your ease.”
sentences.n: fehlen takes the dative of the person who lacks — “es soll euch nicht fehlen,” nothing shall be wanting to you. Bequemlichkeit is ease, comfort.

sentences.t: „Mein Gott,“ sprach der Alte, „wie bist du zu dem Reichthum gekommen?“
sentences.l: “My God,” spoke the old man, “how have you come to this wealth?”
sentences.n: “zu etwas kommen” is to come by something, to acquire it. Reichthum is the 1857 spelling of Reichtum.

sentences.t: Da erzählte er ihm wie alles zugegangen wäre und wie er im Vertrauen auf sein Glück einen so reichen Fang gethan hätte.
sentences.l: Then he told him how everything had gone about and how, in trust upon his luck, he had done so rich a catch.
sentences.i: Then he told him how it had all come about, and how, trusting to his luck, he had made so rich a catch.
sentences.n: “zugehen” is separable, used of how a thing happens or comes about. wäre and hätte are the subjunctives of reported speech, which mark these as the son’s words and not the narrator’s. gethan is the 1857 spelling of getan. “einen Fang thun” is to make a catch, as of fish — the boy has landed something.

sentences.t: Mit dem übrigen Geld aber zog er wieder hin auf die hohe Schule, und lernte weiter, und weil er mit seinem Pflaster alle Wunden heilen konnte, ward er der berühmteste Doctor auf der ganzen Welt.
sentences.l: With the remaining money, however, he moved off again to the high school, and learned further, and because he could heal all wounds with his plaster, he became the most famous doctor in the whole world.
sentences.i: But with the rest of the money he went off again to the university and carried on there; and because he could heal every wound with his plaster, he became the most famous doctor in the whole world.
sentences.n: “hinziehen” is separable — zog … hin, moved off there. “die hohe Schule” is again the university, where the tale began. Doctor is at once the learned man and the healer, which is the point of the ending.

glossary.abgehen: abgehen — to go down (auf und abgehen: to walk up and down; separable ab-)
glossary.alter: das Alter — old age (neuter noun; im Alter: in old age; not the adjective alt)
glossary.an: an — at, on, to; also the separable prefix of ansehen, anfangen, ankommen
glossary.bös: böse — angry, cross (short form of böse; here anger, not wickedness)
glossary.darüber: darüber — about it; over it (sich darüber Gedanken machen: to worry about it)
glossary.entdeckte: entdecken — discovered, caught sight of (3rd sg. preterite)
glossary.es: es — it (neuter pronoun; also clipped onto a word: riefs = rief es, wills = will es, wenns = wenn es)
glossary.fang: der Fang — catch, haul (masc. noun; einen Fang thun: to make a catch)
glossary.gelassen: lassen — let (past participle; heraus gelassen: let out)
glossary.heilen: heilen — to heal, cure (infinitive verb; here the verb, not the adjective heil)
glossary.heller: der Heller — heller, the smallest copper coin (masc. noun; keinen Heller: not a penny; not the adjective hell)
glossary.hieb: der Hieb — blow, stroke (masc. noun; einen Hieb thun: to strike a blow; not the past of hauen)
glossary.hob: heben — lifted, raised (3rd sg. preterite; in die Höhe heben: to lift up)
glossary.ihm: ihm — to him, for him (dative of er)
glossary.ja: ja — yes; (as a particle) indeed, after all
glossary.junge: der Junge — boy, lad (masc. noun, nom. sg.; not the adjective jung)
glossary.jungen: der Junge — boy, lad (masc. noun, dat. sg.; not the adjective jung)
glossary.kehren: kehren — to turn, go (heim kehren: to return home; not kehren, to sweep)
glossary.lappen: der Lappen — rag, cloth (masc. noun; here singular, one rag)
glossary.lebt: leben — live! (2nd pl. imperative, respectful ihr)
glossary.lebtag: der Lebtag — lifetime (dein Lebtag: all your life long; old adverbial accusative)
glossary.lieber: lieb / gern — dear (lieb, inflected: lieber Vater); rather, sooner (comparative of gern)
glossary.packen: packen — to pack (sich heim packen: to take oneself off home; reflexive, rough)
glossary.riefs: riefs — = rief es, it cried (rufen + clitic es)
glossary.schloß: schließen — closed (3rd sg. preterite; sich zusammen schließen: to close up; not das Schloß, castle)
glossary.schneide: die Schneide — cutting edge of a blade (fem. noun; not a form of schneiden)
glossary.schon: schon — (in a promise) sure enough, never fear; also: already
glossary.setze: sich setzen — sit down! (2nd sg. imperative, reflexive: setze dich)
glossary.stahl: der Stahl — steel (masc. noun; not stahl, the past of stehlen)
glossary.stande: der Stand — dative sg. only in the idiom zu Stande bringen: to bring about, accomplish
glossary.verstand: der Verstand — understanding, sense (masc. noun; von etwas keinen Verstand haben: to know nothing of a thing; not the past of verstehen)
glossary.wagen: wagen — to risk, venture (infinitive; ich wills wagen: I will risk it; not der Wagen, carriage)
glossary.weg: der Weg — way, path (masc. noun; not the adverb weg, away)
glossary.weiß: wissen — know, knows (1st/3rd sg. present; not weiß, white)
glossary.wovon: wovon — from what, with what (interrogative, wo- + von)
